ai.literal: Desire not, even if one wins, gambling; even that which was won is like a fish having swallowed the hook's metal.
ai.translation: Do not desire gambling even if you can win. Even what is won is like a fish swallowing the metal hook.
ai.modern: சூதாட்டத்தில் வெற்றி பெற்றாலும் அதனை விரும்பக் கூடாது. அதில் வென்ற பொருளும், மீன் தூண்டிலின் இரும்பை இரை என்று நினைத்து விழுங்குவதைப் போன்றது.
ai.explanation: The couplet warns against the deceptive nature of gambling. It advises never to desire gambling, even if one happens to win initially. The word 'பொன்' here refers to the metal of the fishing hook, not gold. Just as a fish swallows the hook thinking it is food and gets caught, the initial winnings in gambling trap the gambler into ultimate ruin.

ai.literal: Having gained one, who lose a hundred, even for gamblers is there indeed, good having attained, living a way?
ai.translation: Is there any way to attain goodness and live well for gamblers who win one and lose a hundred?
ai.modern: ஒன்றை வென்று நூறை இழக்கின்ற சூதாடிகளுக்கு, நன்மையை அடைந்து வாழக்கூடிய ஒரு வழி இருக்கிறதா? (இல்லை).
ai.explanation: The couplet asks a rhetorical question about the ultimate fate of gamblers. It describes the core nature of gambling as 'gaining one and losing a hundred' (ஒன்று எய்தி நூறு இழக்கும்), emphasizing the inevitable and disproportionate losses that overshadow any minor, occasional wins. The phrase 'உண்டாங்கொல்' (is there indeed?) strongly implies a negative answer. Consequently, the text asserts that attaining goodness and living a stable, prosperous life (நன்று எய்தி வாழ்வது ஓர் ஆறு) is entirely impossible for those addicted to gambling.

ai.literal: Rolling game unceasingly if one calls, wealth income having gone outside indeed will fall.
ai.translation: If one constantly calls the roll in the game of dice, their wealth and income will depart and fall to outsiders.
ai.modern: உருளும் சூதாட்டத்தை இடைவிடாமல் ஆடினால், ஒருவனது பொருளும் வருவாயும் அவனை விட்டு விலகிப் பிறரிடமே சென்று சேரும்.
ai.explanation: The couplet warns against the addiction of gambling. The phrase urul ayam refers to the game of rolling dice, while porul ayam refers to one's accumulated wealth and incoming revenue. If a person constantly calls out the dice rolls without stopping, all their wealth and income will leave them and fall into the hands of outsiders. The play on the word ayam, meaning both a game and income, highlights how engaging in the former destroys the latter.

ai.literal: Misery many having caused, greatness which destroys, than gambling, poverty that which gives one thing is not.
ai.translation: There is nothing that brings poverty more surely than gambling, which causes many miseries and destroys one's greatness.
ai.modern: பல துன்பங்களை உண்டாக்கி ஒருவனது சிறப்பை அழிக்கும் சூதாட்டத்தைப் போல, வறுமையைத் தரும் செயல் வேறொன்றும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: Gambling is described as a destructive force that brings about multiple forms of misery ('சிறுமை பல செய்து'). It ruins a person's reputation, wealth, and greatness ('சீர் அழக்கும்'). Because of these devastating effects, the couplet concludes that there is absolutely nothing else that guarantees poverty as certainly as gambling does.

ai.literal: Dice and gambling hall and hand (skill), having been infatuated, those who desired eagerly, (are) those who became nothing.
ai.translation: Those who become infatuated with and eagerly cling to the dice, the gambling hall, and the skill of their hands, will become utterly destitute.
ai.modern: சூதாடும் கருவி, சூதாடும் இடம், கைத்திறன் ஆகியவற்றின் மேல் மயக்கம் கொண்டு அவற்றை விடாமல் பற்றிக்கொண்டவர்கள், இறுதியில் ஒன்றுமில்லாதவர்களாக அழிந்து போவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: The couplet warns about the destructive nature of gambling. It lists three elements that gamblers become obsessed with: the dice ('கவறு'), the gambling hall ('கழகம்'), and their own sleight of hand or skill ('கை'). Those who become infatuated ('தருக்கி') and eagerly cling to ('இவறியார்') these things will ultimately lose everything and become destitute ('இல்லாகியார்'). The repetition of the 'உம்' (and) suffix emphasizes how these three elements collectively consume the gambler's life.

ai.literal: Belly they-fill-not, suffering they-will-suffer, gambling called by-goddess-of-misfortune those-who-are-covered.
ai.translation: Those enveloped by the goddess of misfortune called gambling will suffer in distress, unable to even fill their bellies.
ai.modern: சூது என்று சொல்லப்படும் மூதேவியால் பீடிக்கப்பட்டவர்கள், வயிறு நிறைய உணவு கிடைக்காமல் வறுமையில் துன்பப்படுவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: The couplet personifies gambling as 'Mukaṭi', the goddess of misfortune and poverty. Those who are completely enveloped or possessed by this destructive habit are said to be covered by her. As a result, they will suffer immense distress and will not even be able to earn enough to fill their bellies with food. The word 'mūṭappaṭṭār' (covered) vividly portrays how gambling completely swallows a person's life, leaving no room for prosperity.

ai.literal: Ancestral wealth and character it will destroy, gambling hall's time if one enters.
ai.translation: If one spends their time entering the gambling hall, it will destroy both their ancestral wealth and their good character.
ai.modern: சூதாடும் இடத்திற்குச் சென்று காலத்தைக் கழித்தால், அது ஒருவருடைய தொன்மையான செல்வத்தையும் நல்ல பண்பையும் அழித்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns about the destructive nature of spending time in gambling halls. The word 'பழகிய' refers to wealth that has been in the family for generations, showing that even deep-rooted prosperity is not safe from this vice. Similarly, 'பண்பும்' highlights that gambling ruins not just material wealth but also one's moral character. Entering the gambling hall ('கழகத்து') and wasting time ('காலை') there will inevitably lead to the total loss of both.

ai.literal: Wealth having destroyed, falsehood having made to undertake, compassion having destroyed, misery will cause to suffer, gambling.
ai.translation: Gambling destroys one's wealth, forces one to embrace falsehood, ruins one's compassion, and inflicts misery.
ai.modern: சூதாட்டம் ஒருவனின் செல்வத்தை அழித்து, அவனைப் பொய் பேசும்படி செய்து, அவனது இரக்க குணத்தையும் கெடுத்து, அவனுக்குத் துன்பத்தை உண்டாக்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet describes the sequential ruin caused by gambling. It begins by destroying a person's wealth, which in turn forces them to embrace falsehood to survive or to keep playing. This deceitful life then destroys their natural compassion for others. The causative verbs emphasize that gambling is an active force that ultimately plunges the gambler into inescapable misery.

ai.literal: Clothing, wealth, food, fame, learning, saying thus, all five, will not reach, gambling if one takes.
ai.translation: Clothing, wealth, food, fame, and learning—all these five will elude one who takes to gambling.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் சூதாட்டத்தை மேற்கொண்டால், உடை, செல்வம், உணவு, புகழ், கல்வி என்று சொல்லப்படும் ஐந்தும் அவனை வந்தடையாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet lists five essential elements of a good life: clothing, wealth, food, fame, and education. The word 'oḷi' (literally light or brightness) is used here in the sense of fame or social respect, while 'āyam' refers to gambling. The poet warns that if a person engages in gambling, these five things will never reach them. Gambling strips a person not only of material necessities like food and clothes, but also of intangible assets like respect and learning.

ai.literal: every time one loses, will desire, gambling indeed, like, sorrow, every time one suffers, it has desire, life
ai.translation: Just as a gambler desires the game even more every time he loses, the soul clings to life with desire every time it suffers sorrow.
ai.modern: சூதாட்டத்தில் பொருளை இழக்க இழக்க அதன்மேல் ஆசை பெருகுவது போல, துன்பத்தை அனுபவிக்க அனுபவிக்க உயிரானது வாழ்வின் மேல் ஆசை கொள்கிறது.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares the soul's attachment to life with a gambler's addiction to the game. Even when a gambler loses everything, his desire to play only increases. Similarly, even when a person experiences continuous sorrow and suffering, the soul does not want to let go, but clings to life with even greater desire. The rhyming words 'இழத்தொறூஉம்' (every time one loses) and 'உழத்தொறூஉம்' (every time one suffers) beautifully parallel this addictive attachment.
